key_insight: Training vision models with a human-inspired developmental visual diet shifts them to rely more on shape than texture, producing substantially more robust visual inference. This provides a resource-efficient route to robust AI vision.
problem_solved: Models trained on conventional datasets often over-rely on texture and are brittle to common corruptions and distribution shifts; the paper addresses how to induce more human-like, shape-based robustness without heavy computational or data costs.
method: Design a developmental visual diet that mimics stages of human visual experience (progressive, structured exposure to visual inputs).
Train standard vision architectures on this curriculum-style dataset instead of conventional shuffled datasets.
Evaluate changes in shape vs. texture bias and test robustness across common corruptions and out-of-distribution scenarios.
impact: Provides ML practitioners a practical, data-centric strategy to improve model robustness and generalization by altering training data ordering and composition rather than increasing model size or compute. This enables more reliable vision systems with lower resource demands.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: staged 'developmental diet' feeding into a standard CNN/transformer, annotated with expected learning phases.
Before/after bar chart: texture vs. shape reliance for baseline vs. developmental-diet-trained model.
Robustness curve: accuracy across increasing corruption severity comparing standard and developmental-diet models.
Iconic timeline or curriculum graphic showing progressive exposure (simple → complex visuals) to convey the training schedule concept.
paper_title: Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust and shape-based AI vision
paper_authors: Zejin Lu, Sushrut Thorat, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Tim C. Kietzmann
